title: Placement: what JS already does in your head

blocks.md:
## No fox yet

Eight short questions about what JavaScript actually does. Wrong answers do not lock you out — they mark which later lessons to take slowly.

Pick the result you expect the language to produce, not the result you wish it produced. Later, the same ideas show up as a fox on a field and as a signal board on a page.

blocks.explainMd: `typeof null` is the string `"object"`. That is a lie the language kept. Later you will treat `null` as its own empty value, not as an object you can poke.

`===` compares kind first. A number and a string are different kinds, so it answers `false` without looking at the contents. Only `==` converts one side before comparing, which is why `0 == ""` is `true` and why you will be told to avoid it.

`if` does not ask "is there a value here", it asks "is this value truthy". `0` is one of the six falsy values (`0`, `""`, `null`, `undefined`, `NaN`, `false`), so the `else` branch runs. This is why counting code that tests `if (count)` silently skips zero.

blocks.promptMd: `function make() { let n = 0; return () => ++n } const a = make(); a(); a();` — `a()` now returns…
blocks.explainMd: `make()` ran once, so `n` was created once. The arrow function returned from it keeps a hold on that same `n` — not a copy of its value. Two earlier calls made it 1 then 2, so this call makes it `3`. Call `make()` a second time and you get a fresh, separate counter.

blocks.promptMd: `const xs = [1]; const ys = xs.map(n => n + 1)` — `xs[0]` is…
blocks.explainMd: `map` builds and returns a new array; it never writes into the one you called it on. `xs` still holds `[1]` and `ys` holds `[2]`. The methods that do change the original are the ones like `push`, `sort`, and `splice`.

blocks.promptMd: A `Promise` that is waiting to finish is in which state?

choices.md: callback — that is the same thing

blocks.explainMd: A promise is in exactly one of three states: **pending** while the work is unfinished, then **fulfilled** with a value or **rejected** with a reason. A callback is not a state — it is one way of being told the work ended. The state is what lets you hand the unfinished result around before it exists.

blocks.promptMd: A plain `function greet() { return this }` called as `greet()` in sloppy Node often sees `this` as…
blocks.explainMd: `this` is decided by how a function is *called*, not where it was written. Called bare, with nothing before the dot, sloppy mode falls back to the global object; `"use strict"` (and every ES module) leaves it `undefined` instead. Call the same function as `obj.greet()` and `this` is `obj`.

choices.md: one element node, or `null` if missing

blocks.explainMd: The page is a tree of objects, not text. `querySelector` hands back the first matching element as a live object you can read and change — or `null` when nothing matches, which is why unchecked results throw "cannot read properties of null". Use `querySelectorAll` when you want every match.

description: A short quiz about what you already expect JavaScript to do. Wrong answers do not lock you out.
